The one who keeps it enjoys heavenly worlds in turn and becomes like the twelve Adityas with the powers of becoming small and so on. Offerings include a cake with the goddess Sanjna.

01-170.json.summary: Sumantu says that one who gives the sun a cow with two faces (a cow with a calf being born) gains chariots like crores of boons, fulfilling all wishes. He becomes like the twelve Adityas and another sun, enjoys vast pleasures until the end of the world, and then becomes all-knowing, pure and established in his own self.

01-171.json.summary: Shatanika asks about the duties of those who serve the sun. Sumantu says one should worship the sun at three twilights and do the fire rite as one can. A Maga should always be devoted to fire and to guests, should earn wealth by right means, and should wear the avyanga girdle. He says all stages of life come from the sun's body. What is done for the Bhojakas is done for the sun, and giving shelter makes one a king. The chapter also says that seeing, honouring and speaking with a devotee each lead to heaven, and that one should not abuse one who is abused or strike one who strikes.

01-172.json.summary: Sumantu says that one who honours a devotee lifts ten generations before and after himself. He speaks of those who see with a calm mind and hate or desire nothing, of the knowers of the Vedas and those who think on the meaning, and of celibacy, austerity, silence, patience and light eating. He says holy places lie between sun and sun, and gives the merit of feeding a devotee of the sun at ancestor rites. A Bhojaka is the sun and the sun is the Bhojaka. He ends by saying the reciters know this duty.

01-173.json.summary: Shatanika tells of a holy conversation that destroys sin and is the best of duties. He says those who remember the sun and sing his praise with devotion wander long in this sorrowful ocean of rebirth, but that their minds are on the sun. The chapter lists the fruits: many fine things, beautiful women with ornaments, beauty, fame, glory and duty. It says giving and offerings to the sun are rare, and that those whose minds are always on the sun are not troubled by Dakinis, Rakshasas and Pishachas. They gain wealth, life, fame, learning and unequalled power.

01-174.json.summary: Aruna speaks about the sun and the beings that depend on him, including the Mothers, gods, Gandharvas, Pishachas, serpents and Rakshasas. He says one who lives without worshipping the sun is lost, while devotees of the sun, who follow his tradition, are untouched by the world like a lotus leaf by water. Among all groups of Brahmins, only a few reach knowledge. The chapter says there is no duty in the three worlds equal to the sun's worship, and ends with a salutation to the eternal, pure lord of the sky.

01-175.json.summary: Garuda speaks about the remedy that removes untimely death and all disease. He gives a hymn to the sun in fire form, with many epithets such as the thousand-eyed and the one with a garland of flames, the one with dark-tawny eyes. It describes the sun with a thousand rays and a seven-horse chariot, and the planets: one with a golden-tawny body and Venus white. He says these great planets are always devoted to the worship of the sun.

01-176.json.summary: Sumantu says that the four-faced lord of the gods is always devoted to the sun's worship. He describes a god in a yellow garment, the beloved of Atreyi, whose body is sacrifice, and a form shining like the moon, with ornaments. It also describes a four-faced god wearing ashes and dwelling in the burning ground, the best of the best and giver of boons, the god of gods and great lord.

01-177.json.summary: Aruna tells of the goddess Mahashveta, who is always dear to the sun and rides a peacock, with a body red as vermilion. She is devoted to the sun and bowed to by Siddhas and Gandharvas and wears all ornaments. He then describes a fierce goddess with a garland of skulls and a staff, and speaks of goddesses honoured at ceremonies of growth. He asks them to bring peace as they delight in worshipping the sun. A goddess with a mark on her forehead and half a moon comes in a calm and radiant form.

01-178.json.summary: Aruna continues the praise and names the gods and beings around the sun. He asks that those who give right and wrong always give steadily. A maiden in fine clothes and ornaments is described, as are the fierce Rudras who live in fearful places, and those in the south-east who are linked with the murder of the steadfast. The gods with the guardians of the quarters are pleased. A beautiful city of Vaivasvata in the south of the great one is described, with a lotus-eyed god in red garlands, and a bright golden girdle.

01-179.json.summary: Aruna names those who worship the sun, including the stars Dhanishtha, Shatabhisha and Purva Bhadrapada, the signs Aries, Leo and Sagittarius, the seven sages up to the Pole Star, and the daughters of sages and unmarried girls. He describes the great serpent Karkotaka, who is full of the strength of poison and is of yellow body. He says that one who recites or hears this list of names with their places gains the reward.

01-180.json.summary: Aruna gives a long list of beings and holy places asked to bring peace through the sun's worship: the Ganga, Yamuna and Narmada rivers, and hosts of Yakshas, Rakshasas and Pishachas. Sumantu says that for one who keeps this peace rite of Aruna, no planetary harm, famine, evil omens or disease will overcome him, and he will be established with sons and grandsons. He lists merits such as that of ten royal consecration sacrifices. He says this holy account was told by the wise sage Vyasa.

01-181.json.summary: Shatanika says that Aruna, the king of birds, was asked this. Anuru, Aruna's brother, speaks on caste and stage of life: the duty that depends on them has four kinds by form, fruit and means. He says right action rests on the Veda. Aruna lists topics such as the placing of officers, the rule of the organs, a short statement of duty and its definition, and duties of Brahma and the gods and of Brahmins. He mentions where a Shudra who is poor may live.

01-182.json.summary: The sun (Aditya) speaks of rites such as the birth rite and the secret naming, and says the many Vedic sayings of the sages may be taken as alternatives. Bhaskara then speaks on marriage: whom one may marry, such as a woman of the same family or a daughter of a maternal uncle, and the marks of a fit bride, such as a swan-like voice, one colour and honey-brown eyes. He describes giving away a daughter, penalties for giving a faulty one, and says nothing in the world is higher than gaining a son. A Kshatriya may also give a daughter, without taking gifts.

01-183.json.summary: Bhaskara says a twice-born should do the five great sacrifices; he gives the three Ashtaka rites and the fourth, and lists kinds of ancestor rites: regular, occasional, for a wish, for growth and the joining of the dead with the ancestors. Aditya says the rite for growth is held at times of prosperity, the new-moon one is called parvana, and others are done at conception, the moon's rite and the hair-parting. He says the yearly rite on the day of death is best of all and should be done with care every year. Anuru then asks how it is done and receives the answer.

01-184.json.summary: This chapter gives rules about gifts to Brahmins and the conduct of Brahmins. It says who should not be given gifts, such as those who do not study, those without sacred fire, and a Brahmin who has taken up the wandering life and returns to women. It lists the amount of alms and warns against food from a Shudra. It says a truthful, pleasant-spoken Brahmin of pure descent is made of all gods and all worlds. It lists penalties and cleansing acts, such as bathing in water from a cow's horns or at a river meeting. A Brahmin who eats forbidden food, such as food of a dead person, honey and meat, falls.

01-185.json.summary: The sun speaks to Anuru about the rite for the ancestors. It describes the gift of food with jaggery and cloth, the way of offering with the left hand, and the six rice balls offered for the mothers. It describes the order of feeding at the rite, with the first vessel and the food prepared. Honour is given to the ancestors, gods and men, and the chapter warns against careless acts such as drinking the rinsing water. It ends with a blessing that givers may grow, along with the Vedas and the family line.

01-186.json.summary: Bhaskara (the sun) continues teaching Anuru on duty and conduct. He lists sacrifices such as the four-monthly rites, the daily fire offering and the animal sacrifice, treats occasional and wish-based rites, and speaks of forbidden food for all classes and impurity from death and birth. He gives the length of impurity, ten days for the twice-born, and rules for the student's life. He ends with the duty of a wife to serve her husband, by which she reaches heaven.

01-187.json.summary: Anuru speaks on the place of faith in duty: duty is always founded in faith and stands in faith from beginning to end. The chapter says the sayings are rules of action and not mere praise. It names the cows Nanda, Subhadra, Surabhi, Sumana and Shobhanavati, and says nectar, the gods' favourite, came from ghee. It says a Bhojaka (the sun's priest), after enjoying many pleasures, is honoured, and that anyone who sees the sun worshipped with devotion gains merit. It ends with the merit of feeding a Bhojaka at a rite for the ancestors.

01-188.json.summary: This chapter is titled the praise of honouring Bhojakas. It says a person who does farming, herding or trade, even with anger and lapses from truth, is not stained if he worships the sun, fire and his teacher. It describes giving of fruit, food and drink with their rewards, and says seeing the sun gives the merit of bathing in the Ganga. It says the ancestors of such a person are pleased as farmers are pleased by a well-ploughed field. Worthy recipients of gifts may be handsome or ugly, clean or dirty, and the one who recites prayers is the best of all.

01-189.json.summary: This chapter is a dialogue on the sun's duties, between the seven-horsed sun and Anuru. It speaks of giving to the poor, blind and wretched, children, old people and the sick, even by compelling those who are unwilling, and of giving at least half a mouthful to seekers. It lists generosity, welcome, friendship and compassion, and the best days for giving, such as days of transition and equinox. It says that faith is the highest gift and the highest austerity. It names great sinners such as killers of Brahmins and drinkers of wine, and says even through low acts, by the sun's power, one may be freed.

01-190.json.summary: This chapter, in the sun and Anuru dialogue, describes the gross heaps of sin that lead to hell. It lists acts such as taking everything from someone in a forest, stealing men, women, elephants and horses, taking sandal, aloe, camphor, musk and silk, violence to young girls, going to low-born women, failing to give what one promised a Brahmin, causing even slight pain in a hermitage, insulting gods, fire, holy people, cows and Brahmins, giving up one's own duty, and cutting down groves. It ends by calling those who do these "minor sinners".

01-191.json.summary: In the dialogue of the sun and Anuru, the sun lists further sins: constant drinking, singing and playing for pleasure, forging orders and deeds, eating food one has cooked without giving to a Brahmin, beating or frightening cows, and certain trades. It lists forbidden items such as ghee and oil taken as drinks, honey, meat, wine, wool, cotton and silk, even in tiny amounts. It names adulterers, thieves and those who act unjustly. It ends by saying that the course after death, according to sin, is threefold.

01-192.json.summary: The sun tells Anuru about the way after death. Those of good deeds, gentle mind and kindness have an easy road, with gifts such as sandals and food seeming to be near them. Those who did not make such gifts must travel through harsh country: falling mountains, forest fires, lions, tigers, biting insects, fierce Dakinis and Rakshasas, rain of burning coals, and bitter cold wind. Those who even slightly worshipped the sun in their minds are spared. He tells all people to keep devotion to the sun.

01-193.json.summary: The sun and Anuru speak about the tooth-stick. The first is of mustard seed, the second of arka leaf cups, and so on in order, with their marks. A sick person is not bound by rules, and a stick of jujube or brihati brings quick relief. An ashvattha stick gives fame and importance among relatives. The user sits at ease in silence, repeats a mantra three times and chews the stick, and if it falls facing away, he repeats it. A student sleeps that night with good rites, then sits down pure, bows to the sun and worships him.

01-194.json.summary: In the dialogue of the sun and Anuru, dreams are described. If a sleeping person sees the sun in a dream, or a water pot, fly-whisk, mirror or gold ornaments, it is good. Further good signs include eating a sheep, a lion or a lotus, winning at dice or war, riding a horse or chariot, beheading oneself (which means a kingdom), killing many (wealth), seizing planets and stars, crossing the ocean, or being eaten by worms (money soon). The chapter also says the number of children and the length of life that certain dream signs show.

01-195.json.summary: The sun and Anuru continue. The sun says the days of the lunar fortnight have their rules, with the third day for neem leaves and the fourth for fruit, and avoiding honey, meat and very sour food. A worshipper follows the rule properly with devotion and worships the sun, with a vessel rich in seven grains and gold. At midday he bathes with a calm mind. If Bhojakas are not available, Brahmins who know the Puranas may be fed. Nothing is hard to get that is not obtained on the seventh day. It ends with a hymn of praise to the sun.

01-196.json.summary: The seven-horsed sun speaks to Anuru. He says that a Bhojaka who gives up property out of greed does wrong. He gives the best rule for offering incense, and for fragrances of four parts mixed, and lists the rewards. He says the seven seventh days described by Vivasvan give the fruit of all sacrifices as the Veda says. A person who gives food to the best Brahmins on the seventh day, and offers flowers such as lotuses, water-lilies and blue lotuses, and worships in Margashirsha and Pausha, reaches heaven. Hearing this with the rule also gives heaven.

01-197.json.summary: The sun tells Anuru more about worship: unequalled lordship and wide fame, flowers of many kinds that quickly free from disease, kimshuka flowers that keep the sun from harming a worshipper, and ashoka flowers that bring eleven kinds of enjoyments. He gives the mantras for worship, with names of the sun at certain points, and a rite of worship with flowers and incense, then circling. After drinking a handful of water, the observer of the seventh day eats whatever he got by the proper payment.

01-198.json.summary: Shatanika asks how Bhishma once questioned Vyasa as he sat on the Ganga's bank. Bhishma asks the sage to tell, as it should be told, about the sun. Vyasa says the sun is called the first of all gods and everything in the world comes from the sun. Brahma is born from his mouth and Rudra from his chest. Bhishma asks why the sun is troubled by Rakshasas at the three twilights. The chapter says duty in the world is shaped toward the sun alone, and the sun guards and creates everything.

01-199.json.summary: Bhishma asks how strength, success, great power and glory come, and Vyasa answers that worshipping the sun by the sun's rule gives them. He describes the way of bathing and worship: bathing with royal honours, rinsing the mouth, offering water, and standing with focused mind in a circle. He mentions raising the vessel to the head and kneeling on the earth. He says even without initiation and mantra, a person who worships with devotion for a year gains the result. He ends by saying this rule of bathing has been told briefly.

01-200.json.summary: Bhishma describes how to worship the sun with a straightened body, placing the heart and other mantras in the body with the word "phat", then the three-syllable sun and the armour. He says by three fierce mantras, one becomes pure in himself. The heart-seed is a matchless place of Brahma. The crest mantra is placed on the crest and the armour on the body. One should regard oneself as the sun, as the wise teach. He asks Vyasa to tell him the full Vedic rule.

01-201.json.summary: Vyasa promises to tell Bhishma a dialogue that increases duty. Vishnu speaks about worshipping the sun called Khasholka, the spotless god, with the heart mantra and the armour. The worship begins at the bright east and goes through the quarters to the north-east, with the verse "ud u tyam jatavedasam". Hymns to the stars and to the unfailing one are given. Vishnu says the worshipper should worship daily with this mantra, and describes the second form worshipped in the bright fortnight and the sixth seed, "hiranyagarbha". He closes with meditation on the god with all marks and ornaments on a diagram.

01-202.json.summary: Vishnu tells how to worship the sun with Vedic verses. He gives a series: the head worshipped with "ishe tva", the feet with "agna ayahi", bathing with "imam me ganga" and with milk using "apyayasva", anointing, bathing with scented water by "vishnor arata", clothes by "brihaspate", incense with guggul by "dhur asi", worship in a lake by "sahasrashirsha purusha", and touching the god's body with "vishvatash chakshus". These verses are fitted to each step of the worship.

01-203.json.summary: Someone asks Brahma for the rule of worshipping the sun in the sky in brief. Brahma says to make an image of gold, silver, copper or stone and worship the sun first, in the middle, with a mantra. The south-west peak is worshipped with the verse "ayam gaur", and the sky seat is always honoured with "salutations to all sins". The worshipper gives clean cloths to a teacher, with many fragrances, flowers and food. One who fasts at the equinox or at an eclipse of the moon or sun and worships properly returns to earth as a king.

01-204.json.summary: Sumantu gives the verses used in sun worship. "Om Khasholka, I call you" is the mantra for the worship, followed by the earth, sky and heaven. The worshipper washes the vessels and fills them from the right source, gives foot water with "hamsah shuchishat", and then offers with "hiranyavarna" and other verses, including incense, the sacred thread with "samudra", and eight verses of the Rig. He says one who always worships the sun in this way, as Brahma and the other gods did, gains the result.

01-205.json.summary: Vyasa continues the rule for worshipping the sun in the diagram. The heart seed is placed in order up to Ishana. One worships the filaments with seedless mantras: foot water, rinsing water, a seat, cloths, perfumes and ornaments. After the sun, the limbs are worshipped with flowers, perfumes and incense. Mars is worshipped in the south-east and the sun's son in the south-west, and then the sun with the guardians of the quarters and planets. The sun in the middle of the disc is the highest truth, and at the end he is released with the heart seed.

01-206.json.summary: Bhishma continues the rules of the worship: the third seed with the visarga, and hand-gestures (mudras). He says that using them one becomes dear to the sun, that the one-syllable mantra cannot be pierced, and that the gesture of the weapon is named. The cow-and-bull gesture shows the divine realm. He describes mantras with "svaha" in the fire offering, and meditation on the sun like a red hibiscus standing on a white lotus, with hands showing the boon and fearlessness, two left hands on the hips and right hands giving fearlessness.

01-207.json.summary: Bhishma says there is no Brahman equal to the sun and no offering equal to the sun's. One should know him as the one god, and even those not wholly devoted to him are helped: kings, thieves, planets, serpents and poverty do not trouble the devotee. The sun is the visible god. A person who worships him on Sunday, or who fasts on the sixth and worships on the seventh, gains all wishes. A seeker of liberation gets liberation or immortality. Sumantu then says how Vyasa and Bhishma went away.

01-208.json.summary: Shatanika asks about the seventh-day vow with tooth-sticks of arka leaf cups and pepper. The vow keeper should be celibate, pure and self-controlled, eating no cooked rice, and keeps it by the rule. Even a person outside the world's rules who does not know the meaning gains wealth lasting seven generations. He lists gold, silver, grain and wealth. A man or woman who keeps the seventh-day vow gains merit like that of pilgrimage baths, gifts and fire offerings, and is free from blindness, leprosy and other defects. A person who fails may make amends and take up the vow again.

01-209.json.summary: Sumantu says that a person who lives on milk, one meal or alms and offers a black-scented milk dish with many fine ornaments gains the fruit of sacrifices with large fees, and is honoured in the sun's world in a fine heavenly chariot. He gives the names of the sun by month, such as Vishnu in Chaitra, Aryaman in Vaishakha, Parjanya in Shravana, Varuna in Bhadrapada, Bhaga in Magha and Tvashta in Phalguna. He ends the rule of incense worship on the seventh day, saying the most secret thing about the lord has been told, and that one who hears it gains joy in this world and honour in the sun's world.

01-210.json.summary: Sumantu tells a story of the seventh-day vow with more rules and examples. A Brahmin who repeats the Savitri a hundred thousand times and keeps the seventh day is to be fed first. The chapter describes the fire rites in the temples, feeding Brahmins after the fire offering, and a king being asked how the sun was worshipped. It mentions a Brahmin whose wife is a Shudra woman, and a woman whose faults are hidden. It says that this seventh-day vow should always be kept with devotion in this way.

01-211.json.summary: Sumantu tells of a man who visited holy places and temples and asked for a way to liberation with little effort. He is told that there is one means and that all who rely on the sun rejoice in heaven. The sage Kauthumi speaks of a third verse to be repeated by one who wants liberation, which is sung by the twice-born at the proper times. The man, by the sun's grace, goes on in a visible form. The chapter ends by praising the holy arka-leaf cup, dear to the sun, which gives wealth.

01-212.json.summary: Sumantu gives the heart, armour and weapon mantras of the sun. He describes a mantra with the syllable "va" as the best nectar, which can bring both blessing and curse by mind, deed and word. He teaches the worship of the one-syllable sun: offering water in a vessel with flowers, binding the worship with the heart mantra, and releasing the god with the heart mantra at the end. The chapter includes the "Om Brahman" weapon mantra, the Gayatri and a line about the cow.

01-213.json.summary: Sumantu says that by doing this, purification of the fire is sure and the god of gods is truly invoked. Then five offerings are given to please the limbs of the god.

01-214.json.summary: Sumantu says that after seven days a worshipper sees the sun and is accomplished. He recites ten thousand times with his mind fixed on the god. By binding the hand-sign described, diseases quickly leave people, and one who sees it does not meet death or sorrow. He describes the hand-signs in detail, with the two hands joined, thumbs up, hands spread or folded, and forefingers bent. One who keeps this goes to the highest place where the sun-god is. Rama is said to have gone with Sita after fasting in this way.

01-215.json.summary: Sumantu gives another rule of worship and the raising of the mantras. He lists the root mantra "Om, salutation to Khasholka" and the Gayatri to Aditya, "Om, we know Aditya, we meditate on the one with a share of all". He gives the directions for placing the forms of the sun: Budha, son of the Moon, in the south, and the sun-self in the east.

01-216.json.summary: Sumantu ends the Brahma part of the Purana with a long account of the reciter and listener. He says a wise person, wanting prosperity, should set up the reciter, and he names those from mixed castes who are not fit. A reciter should sit on a seat that is not too high or too low and one who hears from such a reciter with faith gains merit. The chapter gives rules for the months from Kartika to Kartika, the marks of a good reciter (the scriptures on the tip of his tongue), who purifies a row of diners at gods' and ancestors' rites, and the sin from insulting him. It ends with gifts, and says hearing it gives the reward spoken by Brahma.

02-001.json.summary: This chapter begins the Madhyama parva with a salutation to the lotus-eyed Lord. The sages ask Romaharshani (Suta) about the holy Purana collection. The chapter says it will cover praise of duty, praise of Brahmins and others, the acts of a dying person and the greatness of giving. It says the householder is the source of the three other stages of life, and that wealth and desire come from duty and rest on it, and duty upholds the whole world. It lists virtues such as non-violence, truthfulness and freedom from slander, and mentions the eighty-eight thousand celibate sages and the supreme abode of the yogis.

02-002.json.summary: Suta describes creation. The lord, thinking on himself, brings forth the three qualities, sattva, rajas and tamas, deludes all things with his light, and withdraws beings again. The chapter lists the lower worlds, Patala, Vitala, Atala and Tala, the earth, sky and directions, and the beings that walk on four feet and two feet. Brahma and Vishnu arise from Primal Nature. It also touches on the arrangement of the world's edge, the continents and oceans, and says time at last wears out all that is born in bodies.

02-003.json.summary: Suta describes the higher worlds, from the world of Janas to the world of austerity, each with its extent, and the hymns the Brahman-knowing ascetics sing. He describes the city of Vishnu, shining like crores of suns and hard to approach, from which there is no return, and Mahadeva with the goddess meditated on by the wise. He names the seven great worlds of the earth, and the lower worlds, mentioning Mucukunda, Shankukarna and Namuchi. Ananta is the serpent-formed Janardana, and the dark form of Shiva is time itself.

02-004.json.summary: Suta describes the size and layout of the earth, said to be fifty crores wide and ringed by the ocean. He names the mountains Himavan, Himakuta and Nishadha in the south, and the lands Champaka, Hiranmaya and others in the north, with Vipula in the west and Supashva in the north. He speaks of the sun and moon: the sun moves by day and the moon by night. He gives the order of the planets above the stars, with Mercury and then Venus, and says some days are to be avoided according to the Atharva Veda.

02-005.json.summary: Suta teaches on the Brahmin and on judging people. He calls the purest of the pure and the teacher of teachers, and says a Brahmin should be invited and honoured. He lists types of bad people, such as the sinful, the angry, the wicked, the talkative and the miser. He lists trades and conduct that lower a person: living by temple service, living off a wife's earnings, informers, those who serve a king or a Shudra, and a student who reads without understanding. He also speaks of gifts of books, jewels and horses, and ends with the study of the horoscope at a child's birth.

02-006.json.summary: Suta teaches that on the twelfth, the new moon or a solar transition, one should honour the ancestors, and gives a verse saluting the father as Brahma, the giver of heaven and liberation. He says duty goes on because the world wins by it. He speaks of honouring mother, father, grandfather and teacher, and says the teacher is the form of Brahma and the father the form of Prajapati. Washing with the water from the teacher's feet makes even the Ganga seem less. It ends with the rule that those who care for their grandmother are higher than a hundred mothers.

02-007.json.summary: Suta continues with rules for the hearer of the Purana and the copying of books. He lists pure foods such as rice, barley milk and a milk dish, and says the listener should face the south and the reciter the north. One who does not honour his father or ancestors, he says, falls to hell. He gives rules for the book: a householder should not copy a book except at Mathura, and copying on an ancestor-rite day ruins the family. The best book is thirty-two fingers wide. He names musical modes and ends by speaking of a house without children.

02-008.json.summary: Suta gives rules for teaching and learning. The scripture should not be taught to a person who comes without proper approach, but to the teacher's wise, dutiful and pure son. A person who dies with knowledge unshared, or withholds it, is said to go to a terrible hell. One should not study praises composed by foreigners. The chapter distinguishes the arts of lawful conduct, the science of wealth, the horse science, the law books and practical life, and says a four- or five-syllable mantra purifies. It lists Rudra as the eleventh and the sun as the twelfth, the Trimbaka at the twenty-sixth, and the pure Brahman.

02-009.json.summary: Suta begins the rules for building and dedicating a pond or well and temples. He describes the types of such works as best, middling and lowest, the fire rite before the main ritual, and how to measure a pool of sixty hands. A clay temple is also holy. He says the number of atoms in a god's house are the number of years of reward. A person who keeps water through the hot season lifts a hundred of his family. He closes with rules about measures for places of different size, with a grove of a hundred thousand trees as the best.

02-010.json.summary: Suta gives the rules for planting trees and gardens and starting a house. He mentions pits with milk and wood, offering to the site at the start of house-building, charming with mantras after two days, places not to plant (riverbanks, burning grounds, south of the house), and the results of various trees: tinduka for family growth, pomegranate for a woman, and so on. He gives the months for planting and the rite of desire for trees. He says that around the fig tree a ten-cubit area is holy to Vishnu, and mentions the tulasi, mango and brahma-tree.

02-011.json.summary: Suta gives short rules on dedications. When a well, pond or garden is set up, the rite varies according to the number of trees, and one should not leave a well unfinished. The rite for a pond or a lake or garden should be done once there are more than two thousand trees, and the dedication of a bilva tree is also described. Parched grain and unbroken rice are then given on the head.

02-012.json.summary: Suta gives measurements for images and temples: the proportions of the face, chin, forehead and nose, the head and neck, the fingers and nails, and the cheeks. He describes an image with hands that hold a golden garland, the heights of images of Narasimha and Hayagriva by "tala", and a lotus with the Shrivatsa mark below. Narada and Kapila are shown with folded hands. The best places for images include Avimukta and Dasharna, and he mentions sandal and aloe with bilva and Shriparnika wood.

02-013.json.summary: Suta describes preparing the ground and the fire pits for a sacrifice. He tells how to dig and sprinkle the ground, avoid round and dark forms, and draw the square with a cord. The pit is used for sprouting, Vishnu rites, pilgrimages, entry to battle and other occasions. The belt of the pit differs: for ten thousand offerings, one belt, and seven belts are not praised for a hundred thousand. The corners hold the womb-mark, and a pit without an image is not used. He gives distances of a hand or a hundred.

02-014.json.summary: Suta continues with the rules of large fire sacrifices, such as a king may do with wealth. He mentions peace and nourishing rites, rites for wonders, a hundred thousand and ten million offerings, and the days: two thousand on the second day, one thousand on the third. He says no change should be made across thirty-one days and that one ordinary rite is done each day. He mentions a bali offering at the second great festival and different counts for five, twelve, sixteen and thirty-two days.

02-015.json.summary: Suta continues with the fire rite: the tongue of the fire is made, and the fire is brought; the goddess of speech is invoked as she bathes after her period. He gives seed syllables with dots, the offerings with three sweet things, and where in the flame offerings go, such as into the pericarp. He says the fire pit has parts like a body, with a head at the north-east, ears and eyes, and gives the measures for the crest and the umbrella-shaped form. Twenty-five ghee offerings are made with the root mantra.

02-016.json.summary: Suta describes meditation on the fire god, who holds a power, a svastika and a hand of fearlessness in long arms. He is invoked, set up and shown eight hand-signs, and worshipped with the great-bellied, great-tongued form as the sky. A hymn addresses him as the origin of all beings, who carries them across the ocean of rebirth, calling him Vaishvanara and bearer of offerings, who lights the world as the sun. It praises him as lord of sacrifice and Jatavedas, and ends with the mantra by which an offering is given.

02-017.json.summary: Suta lists the names of the sacred fire for different rites. It is Agni at the fifty, Kashyapa at the other fifty, Varuna for peace, Aruna for destructive rites, Lohita at the food sacrifice, Prajapati for the house-site rite and in the tent and lotus, the sun at the release of a bull, and Rudra at the end. Fire as Kala is for frightening, Kravyada for the burning of the dead, Parthiva for the naming, Shadanana for the tonsure. Jatharagni is in the stomach, the Badava fire in the sea, Varuna the water-fire, Havirbhuj the Brahmin's fire.

02-018.json.summary: Suta gives the measures of items for the fire offering. Parched grain is a fistful, rice flakes measured by the fist, and the size of cakes and fruits, gulancha stems four fingers long, a birch leaf, and a shami twig. He lists sandal, aloe, camphor, musk and saffron, and says to wash the rice and the bilva leaf once, not twice or thrice, or the offerer goes to Rasatala. He warns against milk-rice offerings to other gods. The shapes of leaf offerings are given by fingers.

02-019.json.summary: Suta describes the sacrificial ladles, the sruva and sruch. He says one should fast before making them, avoid meat, take wood and divide it into thirty parts, make the altar shaped like a winnowing basket, and make the ladle of twenty-four parts. He gives measures: the circle is five fingers, the stick eight hands, and the ladle ten tolas. The wood is from the three classes or the moon-tree. A copper ladle is also made but not used there.

02-020.json.summary: Suta continues with the rules for the sacrifice and the number of offerings. He mentions flower offerings, placing two ladles one over the other, and the seer for the verse "purna darvi" as Shatakratu (Indra). Vishvamitra does ten thousand offerings, and the fruits of orange, dhataki and bakula are used. A hundred-thousand offering has six priests, with four more as one can afford, free of envy. A person who does this without desire reaches the highest Brahman and is honoured in Shiva's world by the Vasus, Adityas and Maruts. Gifts are given at the sacraments of the twice-born.

02-021.json.summary: Suta continues the technical rules of ritual diagrams and seats for sacrifices. He gives measures for diagrams of several kinds, including a square one, a diagram shaped like a heron, and a five-seated great throne, and says how they are enlarged for peace-giving rites for the planets. He warns that errors in the order bring fault, so the work should be done carefully. The altar is smeared with cow dung, and the cord and peg must be set with care.

03-001.json.summary: Suta gives measurements for drawing the lotus diagram used in worship: the width of the cord ends, the circles of twelve fingers, the size of the lotus in four parts, and the three kinds of filaments. He says the colours and order follow the same rules as before for installation and for water works. The lotus is drawn with a small wheel at its end and with the leaf tips. One who draws it but does not worship it, or has no fire rite, gains nothing.

03-002.json.summary: Suta describes the heron-shaped diagram and others. He gives how the colours are placed from the east in order, with red used in the south and north. He says the heron stands for Narayana and the tiger for the goddess Tripurasundari. Camphor, saffron and gorochana are used for the colours. A peg is set in the middle with measure of a fist and arm, and rows of footprints are set out. He then describes the "all-round-auspicious" diagram with signs of the zodiac, and the five-lotus diagram marked with four svastikas.

03-003.json.summary: Suta gives the money measures used in ritual payments: eighty cowries make a pana, and pond and lotus-pond works take half of that. He gives the amounts to the king's tax collector, for initiation and in gifts, and says how gold and silver are exchanged. The teacher's share is one part given by the sacrifice-giver. He gives the value of images' fees, from the head or navel of the deity, and for small linga stones a price in gold with a quarter or half for the Shridhara form.

03-004.json.summary: Suta continues with payment amounts for various works. Two silver pieces are given for the all-round-auspicious diagram, a quarter for the heron diagram, and half of that for a six-cornered one. He says to add a pana for each day, and that wages for milking cows are a quarter of a cowrie. A man with a beard and nails to be cut is paid two kakinis. He lists the sizes of wicks and cloths, and says a lamp wick of three or four cubits is best.

03-005.json.summary: Suta gives the rules for the water pots used in the rites. The god is invited into rice and flowers and worshipped. He describes pots that are unbroken, of even shape and filled, made of metal or clay, and the rule of measure for each. A general rule for a sacrifice is given, with the sage Gautama as seer of the mantra and the metre Trishtubh. He lists fruits to be placed in the pot, such as jujube, nagara, amla and neem, and grains: sesame, urad, mung, shyamaka and rice. A flower and sandal are offered with the "Shri" mantra.

03-006.json.summary: Suta explains the calendar. He distinguishes the solar day, the lunar month by tithi and the use of the lunar month at the new moon, full moon and the eight-day rites. He says the sun goes through a sign in a month, that after two and a half years an extra month falls, and that rites such as the king's consecration can be done in the extra month. He tells how a great setting of Venus lasts seventy-two days and how Vishnu sleeps and wakes. It closes with the rising of Durga in the month of Tula.

03-007.json.summary: Suta gives rules on how to choose the day for a rite, with morning and the lunar day given to the gods by Brahma. He says that the tithi at sunrise is taken, that the day on which the lunar day ends at sunset belongs to the ancestors, that a new moon joined with another should not be fasted even by a sage, and that the eleventh with the night is always to be kept. He gives the order for breaking a fast on certain days and rules for sacrifices lasting long, and for the rite for the dead. The chapter also treats Magha and the Sun's pleasure.

03-008.json.summary: Suta gives a long series of rules for fasting and worship by lunar day and month. He names the three kinds of the fourth lunar day, Shiva, Shanta and Sukha, the worship of the eighteen-armed goddess on the bright eighth of Ashvina, and when to break a fast on the twelfth. He explains what to do when the twelfth does not come in time, and says to take a night meal on the dark fortnight. He tells of the fourteenth, called "breaker of pride", in Chaitra, the dark fourteenth of Phalguna, and the full moon of Kartika with the star Bharani. He says one should never eat twice on the new-moon day.

03-009.json.summary: Suta lists the Pravaras, the lines of sages who are named at a Brahmin's fire rite: for example Chyavana, Jamadagni, Aplavana, Atreya, Vasishtha, Aurva, Vishvamitra, Kaushika, Vatsyayana, Angiras and Mitravaruna. He gives the groups of three or five for various families and ends by saying that families not named or not known are counted under Kashyapa.

03-010.json.summary: Suta describes the worship of the gods of the diagram in the great fire rite. He names deities such as water, Savitri, Jaya and Rudra, the colours (smoky yellow, red-yellow, white, black and dark), and a second diagram. He gives the verses and metres with their seers and how to meditate on each god: Indra yellow and mounted on the white Airavata, a two-armed three-eyed god with matted hair, a yellow goddess in red garlands, a red god with upright hair and red clothes, and a dark demon in black garlands. He ends with the gold given in pond-dedication rites.

03-011.json.summary: Suta continues with the worship of the gods placed around the fire. He mentions Rudra and the king's wasting disease placed at the left hand, the sun as the god, the seer Pushpadanta, the metre Trishtubh, and a conch-coloured two-armed god with a discus, with the mantras of the seers Gandha and Garga. He says a Brahmin may offer fifty oblations with sesame or rice. He assigns offerings to the gods: honeyed rice for Soma and a jaggery cake for Naga. The chapter ends by praising those who always meditate on the endless Achyuta in the lotus of the heart.

03-012.json.summary: Suta describes the pot rite for the earth. He says that one worships Brahma and the earth-bearer at the hole, gives an unbroken pot of five colours, and offers water, milk, ghee and honey with the rule. A pair of fish and a pair of sheep are released, a figure of urad paste with red flowers is made, and gold and a cow are given to the Brahmin. The final bathing is done while reciting "may this be well-placed". He lists forbidden items such as milk, astringents, fried vegetables, jujube and sesame.

03-013.json.summary: Suta gives details of the first parts of the fire rite: sweeping of the ground, the seers of mantras, the placing of the first stick, sending away the fire that eats flesh, the entry of Brahma with two mantras, and a prayer that the oceans be pleased. He lists foods offered: jackfruit, coconut, sweets. The teacher cuts the Pinjuli and the purifier. He mentions the dice being removed, the earth heated again, the sprinkling water set on the north, and the water pot carried in the left hand.

03-014.json.summary: Suta says the opening rites apply to all fire offerings: the offerings with the verses "ayash cagne" and "ye te shatam", one for Prajapati and one for the Svishtakrit fire. Other cases are done in the reverse order with "svaha". He explains how to join regular and occasional rites in one day, with the ghee offerings first, how marriage rites of the twice-born are done, and how to handle a goat offering. He gives rules for offerings to the sun, and notes a five-fruit sign on the palm.

03-015.json.summary: Suta describes the forms of the seven flames of the fire god for meditation: the first is golden, with a flame as tongue, of great brightness; another is gold, two-armed and white, holding kusha grass; another red like the rising moon with four arms, one dark like black eye-paint holding a golden pot on the left, one shining with her hands joined, and one like the red hibiscus with many forms. A final verse addresses the blue-lotus-like goddess. The chapter ends with how to look at the place and dig it with a mantra.

03-016.json.summary: Suta gives rules for the specific forms of the sacrifice. He says Shaiva for Shiva and Varuna for a water-shed, with a pair of mantras, special rules for the sacrificial post, and the verses "you are a Gandharva" and "his foot". He describes how to invite the god, using five Brahmins, how to churn the fire, the sand altar a cubit wide, and a ten-finger measure. In the dark fortnight, oleander and bilva fruits are used in the rite of the three cities.

03-017.json.summary: Suta gives the rules for honouring the officiating priest and for gifts. A worthy recipient is given the respectful offering first and then the vessel. He lists who is not fit to receive: one with a bad nail, an adulterer and others. A prayer asks for lasting fame as long as the moving and unmoving worlds endure. The god is worshipped with perfumes, flowers and a pair of cloths. He says that desire should not be too strong and that being without desire is not good either. For the great vow and installations, copper or golden vessels are used.

03-018.json.summary: Suta says that the pure second, third and thirteenth lunar days are good for installing life in a pond or similar work. He describes the tent: a round shed of sixteen cubits on a gently sloping site, decorated with many garlands and cloths, with flags in the directions and at the doors, and with plantain trees. The fire pit is made with an inner belt, with nine pits in the pit-rule, placed at the corners of the altar. The pots are covered with garlands and cloths, full of water and with gold inside.

03-019.json.summary: Suta gives a very long and detailed rule for installing a god, covering the making of the god's image and the offerings. The chapter lists the nine kinds of rites and the thirty parts, forms of the god such as Gomukha and Nandabhadra, and describes the god on a lion throne with blue-lotus eyes, two arms, a noose in his hand and a handsome form. It mentions the mantra "tryambaka" worshipped with honey and milk-rice, three sticks of palasha or ashvattha, the seven planets, and offering with the five jewels and a conch. At the end, the house worship is done and Brahmins are fed.

03-020.json.summary: Suta continues the installation: the rite of the Vedic tradition, with the musical sound of instruments leading the Brahmins; three pots placed in each direction from the east; the Varuna tune; and offerings to Mars of milk and rice. The god is worshipped with the verse "sahasrashirsha" and the offering is carried away. Honey, ghee and jaggery are mixed with parched grain for the fire. A fine couch is made on the north of the tent. Varuna is placed in the middle of the water of the pond, then the lamp-waving is done. At the end Narayana is given to the Brahmin.

04-001.json.summary: Suta continues with the installation of works such as ponds and gardens. He mentions placing Mandara on the east above the gateway, a ghee lamp, guggul and sarala incense for the god, worship of Ishana, Tatpurusha and Vayu in the directions, and one ghee oblation to each in turn. Honey, milk and barley are offered in a cooked-food rite. A sharp needle is used on a pair of pots. At the end a cow, gold and grain are given to the teacher. He names Hayagriva, Madhava and Purushottama, and says that Vishvakarma, as white as crystal, is placed on the left.

04-002.json.summary: Suta gives more rules for installing a pond or tank. He says the worship of Rudra with the five parts, grain, cloth and a fee frees a person from all sins and gives honour in Vishnu's world, where he stays as long as the merit lasts without falling. The lord of Rakshasas, standing on a platform with a sword in his hand, is addressed to prevent harm to animals. If creatures die from injury and similar faults, a cooked-food rite is done. The chapter ends with how to wrap the post with a stream of milk and pour a stream of ghee.

04-003.json.summary: Suta describes the setting up of a pot with Vishnu and Soma worshipped, decorating trees with garlands and ornaments, and feeding five Brahmins. A post is set in the middle and a plantain tree planted. Eight and eight offerings are made, and others with ghee. A fee is given and the full offering is made. He then gives the rule for dedicating a single tree among trees: Dharma, the earth and the people are worshipped at the root, and a cow and fee are given as a ritual of "desire" for the tree.

04-004.json.summary: Suta gives the next rules: durva grass and rice are offered for a Brahmin feast of three. He describes a two-armed god with a trident and all ornaments, the same giving of vessels as before, and the principles of earth, sky and heaven. A leaf of five black seeds the size of a large knot is made. One oblation each is made with flowers, sesame and ghee, with the Vedic verse "imam varuna". Barley milk is given to the directions' lords and milk rice to others. The rite ends with a fee, the full offering and wrapping with a red cord in four turns.

04-005.json.summary: Suta gives the rule for dedicating a garden. The sun and Vishnu are worshipped in a pot, and Mandara and the others are invited and honoured in order. Ananta is worshipped between the south-west and west, with Vasudeva, Brihaspati and a lord of the circle. Soma is meditated on as four-faced and white as crystal. One oblation each is given to the seven tongues of the fire, with Vedic verses, and at the end a cow, an iron vessel and the fee are given.

04-006.json.summary: Suta repeats a short rule: a pot is set up, Soma and Vishnu are worshipped, the trees are decorated with garlands and ornaments, five Brahmins are fed, a post is set in the middle with a plantain tree, and eight and eight oblations are made. The fee is given, the full offering is made and the sacrificer goes home. The chapter is marked as the sixth chapter of the third part of the Madhyama parva.

04-007.json.summary: Suta describes planting a tree: the tree is set up first and bound with thread. Sesame and barley offerings are made eight and eight times by the rule. Dharma, the earth and the people are worshipped at the root, and a cow and fee are given. The "desire rite" is the worship of the tree.

04-008.json.summary: Suta gives the rule for a lotus-diagram rite. A lotus is set out, general water offering is made, a pot of water is placed, and durva grass and rice are offered with three Brahmins fed. Vinayaka is worshipped in one pot, Brahma in another, and Shiva in the diagram, with worship of the seat first. A two-armed god with a trident is described. Offerings are made to Rudra by the number of Rudras. A plantain tree is planted, the teacher is satisfied and a stream of milk is poured.

04-009.json.summary: Suta gives a short rule: after worshipping Ganesha, Shiva and Vishnu, a cooked-food offering is made, a barley-milk offering is given, and the sacrificer releases the dedication with a spoken sentence. The Yakshas, Nagas, Gandharvas, Siddhas and Maruts are named.

04-010.json.summary: Suta describes a further rite: worship of Rudra, of Durga in the middle, and of the lord of wealth. Seven Brahmin couples are fed at home. The tree is wrapped with cloth. Shiva is made leader and the Adityas are placed at the leaf and root; the guardian of the forest, Soma, the sun and the earth are named. Gold, a bronze vessel, betel and a copper vessel are given. He then gives the rule of installation at night with five or seven pots decorated with perfumed oil, the Vishnu hymn, vermilion and sandal, five oblations, the sacrificial post and the full offering, and feeding Brahmin couples.

04-011.json.summary: Suta says that the person who does this lives in heaven for sixty thousand years. After completing the daily rite he worships five Brahmins, does the fire rite and gives a fee to a Brahmin.

04-012.json.summary: Suta gives the rule for the day before the preparation: a pot is placed at a good time. Oil is used with the verse "akrishnena", and sandal with "shri cha te". In the morning, a rite for the ancestors for prosperity is done. The ground diagram is drawn in the middle of the altar by the kings. Ganesha, the planets and the guardians of the quarters are worshipped in the pot. Vastoshpati is worshipped with sandal and perfume. The fee is given, water is offered to the sun, a pot is placed on the tent and ghee offered.

04-013.json.summary: Suta describes worshipping Varuna in a white pot at the west of a well for travellers. A cloth, food offering, lamp and sandal are given. One feeds a couple and chooses one Brahmin. A kusha-grass rite is done in the cooked-food manner, one oblation is given to others with the ladle, and five oblations are made with certain verses. Offerings are also made to Mahadeva and Ishana. He then says he will explain installing a small well in a tent, which is wrapped with red thread and gets a post.

04-014.json.summary: Suta says that on the day before the preparation, Brahmins are fed as the rule says, Narayana is offered honey and milk-rice on the altar, and the work is wrapped with red thread and a fee is given. A post is set in the north-east. Grain, barley and wheat are given to the Brahmin with a fee.

04-015.json.summary: Suta gives rules for a bathing rite with the Gayatri and other mantras. Flowers, fruit and ointment are offered with verses. The sacrificer then wraps the work and goes home, completes the ancestor rite with worship of the Mothers, and the teacher is the priest. Rudras and Vasus are worshipped around the pot. A hundred and eight offerings are made, and others as one can afford. The fee is gold, sesame and grain with flowers. He names trees including the Soma tree, Jayanti and the bilva.

04-016.json.summary: Suta describes the rite for a bridge or dam, and for a grain mountain gift. A pot is set at night the day before and worshipped, with perfume, sandal and the mantra "shri cha te lakshmi". Eyeliner and lac are applied. The best priest is called Varaha, and five ghee offerings are made to Varaha. Rice with urad and the best food are given for the people and for the earth. The sacrificer gives the post and flags with a mantra at the end. Brahmins are fed in the morning, twenty-eight at a time.

04-017.json.summary: Suta gives the rules for giving a cow without ornaments (half the fruit) and for halving the gifts. Ganesha, the field-guardian, Shesha and the guardians of the directions are worshipped with a cooked-food rite, and Brahmins are fed at the end. The post is made, and the whole thing is made three cubits by the rule. The verse "tad vishnoh" is used with pot water, and Vastoshpati and Vishnu are worshipped at the post. He ends with a prayer about all the grass and shrubs on the earth.

04-018.json.summary: Suta says that after the sun's northward course, when it has passed, there are thirty-two kinds of images of Narayana and others. The wise person does the daily rite and then a rite for prosperity. Ganesha, the planets and the guardians of the quarters are worshipped in each pot. The god is bathed first with five kinds of water, oils, fats and astringents, and the leaf, flower and three-leaf offerings of tulasi are named. Clay from an elephant's tusk and a horse's hoof is used. Then life is installed in the image and a fire rite is done.

04-019.json.summary: Suta describes giving a hundred oblations with bilva leaves or fruit, and feeding and bathing the god with scented water for three days. He then explains the installation of a linga of Shiva according to the Tantra rule, with worship of the retinue, measures of the linga, and a pot with Prajapati and a white lotus. Sun, Ganesha and Brahma are worshipped. It may be hidden for one or three days, and a rule about animal knowledge is given for six months. He says to give animals if one has wealth.

04-020.json.summary: Suta gives a long list of omens and signs that portend good or bad for a house or kingdom. They include a white owl, a crow and a cuckoo; a fire in the house without a flame; a shower of gold or flowers; a tree suddenly bearing fruit; swans or frogs in a house; ruin of a king or death of a vehicle; and what rites remove the evil. It then describes the many-sided rules for binding animals in a forest, village or town, and offerings to the planets and to Tryambaka and Dhananjaya.

05-001.json.summary: This chapter opens the Pratisarga parva. The sages ask which kings ruled in the twenty-eighth Satya age, and Suta answers with a list of kings, each said to rule a hundred or a thousand years less than the one before. Names include Ripunjaya, Prasenajit, Prishadashva, Trishanva, Sagara, Dilipa, Ambarisha, Sudasa and Dasharatha. A king gains a divine vehicle by Brahma's boon, and the Satya age is said to be full of duty in Sagara's time. In Dasharatha's time a drought comes, the goddess Mahakali speaks to a king in a dream, and the islands of the western sea are lost.

05-002.json.summary: Suta continues the list of kings, saying that each ruled like his father or for a stated number of years. Names include Sudarshana, Aja, Kusha, Kshemadhanva, Vajranabhi, Svarnanabhi, Mahashva, Keshinara, Dharmaraja and Shakyavardhana, who are called descendants of Raghu. Kurukshetra is said to have been made by one of them. Men are said to become fewer from the start of the third quarter of the Treta age. The line goes on through Budha, Ayu, who is made a python by a curse of Durvasas and freed by Vishnu's grace, and Chitraratha, Kamalamshu and Vidarbha, who reign ten thousand years and go to heaven.

05-003.json.summary: Shaunaka and Suta continue the list of kings. Each is said to rule as his father did, or a hundred years less, and the names include Atithivardhana, Dhanapala, Saumadatti, Dushyanta, Shakrahotra, Dhanurdipta, Vikriti, Devaratha, Sattvavan, Dilipa and Suyodhana, who ruled sixty years. The land of Bharata and the field of Kurukshetra are mentioned. One of the line is born to Vasudeva and Devaki. The chapter ends with Yajnadatta, Sunitha, Medhavi and Ahinara. One king is killed by foreigners (Mlecchas) and goes to Yama's world. A foreigners' sacrifice is held, and they are killed.

05-004.json.summary: Shaunaka and Suta continue. A pleased king honours a Brahmin, and an angry king who knows the Veda is mentioned. The kings of the Huns, Barbaras, Shakas and Khasas are named, and the king gives Brahmins their fee and is consecrated. A prayer salutes Vasudeva, the witness through the four ages, who lives in the field of the kalpa and loves his devotees. Two born of Vishnu and Kardama increase the foreign lines. Kings are named with reign lengths such as nine hundred and thirty years, three hundred and sixty-five years and seven hundred years, including Anuhasta, Virada and Lomaka. Three sons, Sima, Shama and Bhava, are born. Nyuha is told that a flood will come on the seventh day, a great rain falls for forty days, and he boards a ship with his family while the rest are destroyed.

05-005.json.summary: Shaunaka and Suta continue with Nyuha's line. The names given include Sima, Hama and Yakuta, and a list of sons and peoples such as Jumra, Kanabja, Rifata, Ilisha, Taralisha, Akkada and Vavuna, with Nimaruha called mighty. Descendants follow, each ruling like his father, including Jujja and Tahara. The line is said to be remembered by name only. Vyasa tells that the people meditated for two hundred years. When the second thousand years of the Kali age comes, the foreigner lines grow, and Vedic worship and speech are lost except at Brahmavarta and on the Sarasvati bank. The chapter lists words that look like English, such as "Sunday" and "February". The sages weep on hearing it.

05-006.json.summary: Shaunaka and Suta continue. Foreigners come, and a man named Kashyapa with his wife Aryavati has ten sinless sons, including Upadhyaya, Dikshita, Pathaka, Shukla and Mishra. Kashyapa reaches Kashmir and the goddess Sarasvati, whom he praises as destroyer of pride and delusion. By her grace ten thousand Brahmins go with him to the land of the Aryas. His descendants rule, and he installs his son Magadha and goes to meditate on Vishnu after bowing to Suta. Regions of the land are named, and kings listed: Kakavarman, Ajatashatru, Nanda, Pranandha, Devananda, and Bindusara who ruled sixty years. Hari is remembered by Kali and takes Buddhist teaching to the city. Four Kshatriyas arise from Vedic mantras, and Ashoka is brought under their control and the Buddhists are destroyed. A king, Pramara, of Avanti is named.

05-007.json.summary: Suta tells of a king who destroyed the Buddhists and became happy and strong. The city of Ajmer is described, and a king named Shukla goes to the Anarta country. Shaunaka asks about the kings born of fire. Pramara reigned six years, followed by his son Devapi, Gandharvasena for fifty years, and Shankha for thirty. After Gandharvasena, a jewel of a son is born, with drums sounding and pleasant winds. The father names him Vikramaditya, for the destruction of the Shakas and the growth of Aryan duty. At five he goes to the forest to do austerity, then goes to the city of Ambavati. Shiva sends him a gift and he takes up the throne. Once, at Mahakaleshvara, he builds an assembly hall of duty, and a being called Vetala sits and offers to tell a great tale.

06-001.json.summary: Suta begins the Vetala stories, told to King Vikrama. King Pratapamukuta has a son Vajramukuta, whose friend is a minister's son. Vajramukuta sees a lovely forest and Padmavati, daughter of Dantavaktra. She takes a lotus from her head and puts it on her ear, a sign that is read as a message. The minister's son, clever and skilled, wins her over, and Vajramukuta gets her. A matted-haired ascetic is mentioned who says his teacher stays in the burning ground and a mantra was set there. At the end Vetala puts a question about duty and a woman who left her faultless bride, which the king answers.

06-002.json.summary: Suta tells a Vetala story set on the Yamuna bank at Dharmasthali, where King Gunadhipa rules. His sister Madhumati is named, and a wise young man, Vamana, goes to Kashi to study. Three Brahmins, Vamana, Trivikrama and Keshava, with the names Harisharma and Satyashila, love the girl Sushila. On a day in Magha, the auspicious time is set. The girl dies and Harisharma does all the rites. Trivikrama grieves much, and Keshava takes her bones. At Sarayu a Brahmin named Ramasharma, devoted to Shiva, with his wife Vishalakshi, brings a dead child back to life with a mantra. The bones are given to a Brahmin, who revives the girl. Vetala asks Vikramaditya which of them should have her, and he answers that the one who gave life is like a father.

06-003.json.summary: Suta tells of a story set in the city of Vardhavan. Vidvanmala, devoted to her husband, is named. A man gives a thousand gold pieces a day, spends part, and keeps the rest. To test him, a crying woman is sent to the burning ground, and the hero Viravara, skilled in weapons, goes toward the sound and speaks gently. Rajalakshmi says she will die at the end of the month, and the goddess says the head of his son must be offered to Chandika. His faithful wife and his son agree. Viravara cuts off his son's head, and the king, seeing all, is moved. The pleased goddess restores the king and grants a boon, and Viravara's family live.

06-004.json.summary: Suta tells the story of King Rupavarman and a bird in a fine cage at his house. Chandravati, the daughter of the king of Magadha, is mentioned, and a salutation to Shiva, the calm giver of wishes. A Brahmin speaks, and Chandravati prays to Durga, who gives wishes. Marriage is arranged in a month. Menaka says to the king that marriages are of this kind. A childless man who performs sacrifices and has a devoted wife is mentioned. A son loses wealth by wrong paths, tells his father robbers took it, and murders his wife for her ornaments. Shridatta goes on trade to Kurukshetra and returns after three months. A thief called Kaphalla sees the cause. Vikrama answers that a woman is more sinful and the man less guilty.

06-005.json.summary: Suta tells of a story in Ujjayini. The messenger Haridasa is a devotee of Hari. His beautiful lotus-eyed daughter asks her father to listen, and he goes to King Harishchandra of the Telugu country. The king asks when Kali will come, and Haridasa answers: when duty told in the Veda is seen reversed, when the rich fall under greed, the Shudras rise, and the earth is barren. A clever Brahmin, a wise Mukunda (Haridasa's son) and the learned Vamana, who shoots by sound, are rivals for the daughter, who is carried off by a Rakshasa to the Vindhya mountain. They fly in a swift chariot given by the goddess. One kills the Rakshasa with an arrow. The three quarrel over the girl, and Vetala's question is who is fit for her. The answer is that the one who kills the Rakshasa is fit.

06-006.json.summary: Suta tells a Vetala story of King Dharmashila, who has a minister named Andhaka, skilled in logic. Durga is set up by Dharmashila, and at midnight Mahagauri tells him to choose a boon. He praises her as Mahalakshmi and Mahakali and is promised a strong, mighty son. A man goes with Kashidasa to the village of Dharmapura, and meets a girl tired on the road with her father. A lovesick man prays to Chandika, and the girl, the daughter of a washerman, is married after the father is deluded. Kashidasa hears and hurries. A woman offers her head to the goddess and takes the form of the goddess. The goddess grants a boon. A woman asks to be given back her husband, and a fine head was cut by her from two people.

06-007.json.summary: Suta tells of Champapuri, where King Champakesha has a daughter Trilokasundari, with deer eyes, cuckoo voice and a soft body. At her bride-choosing, many kings come, and four of them, called Indra, Yama, Kubera and Varuna, each speak to the king. They are said to be a man bringing jewels for sacrifice, a man for the fire offering and a man for good food each day. The king is bewildered, and the goddess, ashamed, is deluded by fate. Vetala laughs and asks the king. The answer is that the Brahmin who knows all the scriptures is a Brahmin by class, but the one who knows the arts is a Shudra, and the one who knows archery is the king.

06-008.json.summary: Suta tells another Vetala story. King Gunadhipa, rich in wealth and grain, lives in Mithila country for his livelihood. He goes hunting, follows a tiger's track, and, faint with hunger, kills a deer. A man in the story tells the king he has eaten a thousand coins of his and asks a hundred coins a month for his family. At the sea shore the king sees an image of a goddess, a Gandharva's daughter, who speaks to a lover. A woman asks the king to take her in a Gandharva marriage, and the king's servant Chirandeva is also named. She is ashamed when the king says Chirandeva is like a son to him and that she is like a daughter-in-law. Vetala asks the king a question on the highest duty of kings and the servant's deed.

06-009.json.summary: Suta tells a Vetala story set in Kamapura, where Virasimha is king. A proud merchant, Hiranyadatta, lives there, and a woman who loves flowers walks past a strong man, Dharmadatta's son. In a lonely place she tells him politely that she will go to him on the tenth day after her marriage. He agrees, leaves her and goes home. On the ninth day her husband seizes her by force. She weeps, and a friend asks the reason. She says she is bound by her promise and goes at night to him. On the way a thief asks for her ornaments. She tells him what happened, he lets her pass, and she goes to the man. Fear of widowhood brings her back to her friend, and the thief gives her up out of fear of truth. Vetala asks which of them acted best.

06-010.json.summary: Suta tells of the dutiful king Gunashekhara. Once he goes to Shiva's temple and a scorpion stings him in anger. A fearless man draws the poison out, and speaks about six inner enemies: delusion, pride, arrogance, possessiveness, desire and blame. He says that Vishnu, Rudra and Brahma are bound by illusion, and that the true Jina, who is non-dual and spotless, is not conquered. He teaches worship of the cow, no harm to creatures, and no meat or drink, and the king takes up the Jain way. His grieving queen takes refuge in Shiva and by Rudra's boon bears a fine son. Gunashekhara dies and goes to hell, while his father gets heaven by his son's duty. The king is later at ease in spring with his queens, and a wife faints when he hands her a lotus. The story ends with the Vedic duty being named as the chief one and the householder living like an ascetic being praised in the Jain books.

06-011.json.summary: Suta tells of Punyapura, where the minister is Satyaprakasha. The king asks how many kinds of joy exist, and is told that the joy of a student is Brahma's joy, that of a forest-dweller is a lesser joy of duty, and that of a renouncer is Shiva's joy, the best. He says there is no joy without a wife in the householder's life, and tells his minister to look for a fitting woman. The minister goes from place to place and finds a girl sitting on a golden tree in the water. The king goes to the sea shore and tells her he has come for her. She says on the fourteenth of the dark fortnight a Rakshasa with a crane vehicle will take her. The king kills the Rakshasa and she says she is the daughter of a Vidyadhara. A great festival follows in the city. It ends with the saying that a king who is a sensualist ruins his kingdom.

06-012.json.summary: Suta tells that Devasvami, a Brahmin who knows the Vedas, worshipped Shiva for a son, and a strong boy named Harisvami was born with a share of the gods. His wife, Rupalavanyika, is as lovely as a goddess. Once in spring with her husband, a Gandharva called Sukala is taken by her beauty. The husband wakes and searches for her, then gives up all sense objects and meditates on Hari. Under a banyan tree an ascetic comes, eats milk-rice that was poisoned and dies, going to Shiva's world. Vetala asks the king who bears the sin of killing a Brahmin. The king answers that a Brahmin gave alms to a hungry man out of fate's confusion, that a person must always suffer the sin he has done himself, and that the sin falls on the one who gave the poison.

06-013.json.summary: Suta tells of a merchant named Dharmadhvaja and a man-eating Rakshasa named Vashara. A pleased Rakshasa speaks to his devotee. A pit is made that confuses men's minds, and a thief steals from the king's house at night and hides the goods in the pit. The guards are deluded by the Rakshasa woman's magic. A man says he is a thief and offers the king a share. At midnight the thief tells the king to go home, as the Rakshasa will eat all men that night. The king brings his wealth and the women. The thief is paraded through the town on a donkey with drumbeats and is to be impaled. The king's daughter, deluded by divine illusion, appears, and the goddess Durga is pleased and revives both. The king explains why the man wept and then laughed.

06-014.json.summary: Suta tells of Chandraprabha, a lovely wife who goes to a flowery wood with her friends and is entranced, and a Brahmin who falls to the ground. A Brahmin sees the beautiful young woman and tells her sorrow to another. A twelve-year-old girl is named. Sudeva, a fine Brahmin, is always in her heart, and he tells her that if she is meant for the best Brahmin, a child will come in four months. A minister's son, deluded by a woman's form, embraces her. A minister named Rajakara has a son Madanalasa. The king gives the bride with wealth by Vedic rule, and Shashi takes the king's daughter home. Vetala asks the king whom the girl belongs to, and the king answers that a field belongs to the farmer and not to the seed-giver. Madanalasa then praises Govinda with a hymn, is freed, and embraces his wife joyfully.

06-015.json.summary: Suta tells of a generous Brahmin at Kanyakubja who asks what to do about his poverty. By the goddess's grace a son named Jimutaketu becomes lord of the Vidyadharas and lives for years in divine pleasures. In an earlier life he was a king in the middle country who hunted, kept a night vigil in Valmiki's hut and heard the story of Rama. A tree speaks to him. On the Malaya mountain a girl called Kamalakshi lives at a Shiva temple, and Jimutavahana, struck by love at the sight of her, prays to the god of love. He is given Vishvavasu as a prince. Jimutavahana weeps where an old woman is grieving for her son who is to be eaten by Garuda. Garuda takes him through the sky, and the girl sees him in the air. Garuda hears him say he came to save the old woman's son, and the god vanishes. Vetala puts a question, and the story ends with Shankhachuda going against his enemy.

06-016.json.summary: Suta tells of a merchant, Ratnadatta, who knows duty and is rich. Seeing a woman's lovely form, he says to the king: "Take her, ocean of kindness, she is made fit for you." King Chandrashekhara, called to counsel his minister Vidura, goes home. He worships with incense, lamps and flowers, and a woman wails in fear. He kills a tiger and rejoices. He goes to the temple of Kamavaruthini, whose image will bring delusion on the king, so he does not marry. A woman who was Balabhadra's wife is named. The king, struck by Kama's arrow, faints and falls. A man says the woman is the daughter of Ratnadatta and the wife of his servant, fit for the king. The angry king says he would go to hell if he took her. The army chief is burnt to ashes. Vetala asks whose merit is greater, and the answer is that the king who conquers desire and keeps duty is greater.

06-017.json.summary: Suta tells of King Mahasena of Ujjayini. His son Gunakara loves wine and meat, is abandoned by his relatives and wanders the earth. A yogi, Kapardin, honours him with a meal from skulls, and calls a Yakshini for hospitality. In the morning she goes to Kailasa. Kapardin teaches him the knowledge that draws a Yakshini. He recites the mantra but the lovely goddess does not come. He lives at home with his parents at night, then goes to Pratibodhi's forest and becomes his pupil. He asks why his beloved Yakshini was not obtained. The answer is that action for success is of three kinds, of the body, of speech and of mind, all three together bring success in this life, and so seekers should do all three. The sage praises him.

06-018.json.summary: Suta tells of a just and generous man devoted to Shiva, and his lovely daughter Dhanavati. In time her daughter Mohini is born, and Dhanavati, widowed and without money, lives at her father's house. A Brahmin named Nyayasharma, who stole a Brahmin's property, is mentioned. A merchant's daughter touches the hand of a man who cries out for Rama, Krishna, Pradyumna and Aniruddha. A Brahmin says he is on the stake for three days. Dhanavati marries her daughter Mohini to him, and he dies and goes to Yama's world. Mohini, young and at her mother's house, is told a verse by a Brahmin asking who sleeps and who wakes, and the Brahmins cannot answer. A kindly sage tells her that beings die and are born every day, and describes how desire arises from resolve and greed from desire. Shiva instructs a king who wants a son. A child with three hands is born and the king is amazed. Vetala says a learned man who wants money is like a teacher.

06-019.json.summary: Suta tells of King Rupadatta of Chitrakuta. At noon on a lake shore, a sage's son sees a girl, their eyes meeting, and the king gains knowledge at the sight. A wise sage tells the king duty that includes compassion: take punishment from the unworthy and gain the fruit of worshipping the worthy, truth in worship of the gods, self-control in worship of the teacher. The sage gives his daughter to the king and goes home. A Rakshasa wants to eat the king's wife and asks for a seven-year-old Brahmin boy to be given for him. The boy laughs loudly at the time of death. The middle son, knowing this, takes refuge in the king, and a Shiva devotee laughs when he sees the king with a sword in hand. Vetala asks why.

06-020.json.summary: Suta tells a Vetala story of a village merchant, Arthadatta, who is busy in trade and gives his daughter in marriage to a merchant named Suvarna. By chance a fine Brahmin comes to the house of Anangamanjari. After a fire offering, a lovely woman's daughter goes to clean, and the girl, her eyes unsteady with passion, gives the Brahmin an appointment. At midnight she waits for him, but by fate he does not come, and she dies. The Brahmin, seeing her lifeless, also dies. Suvarna comes and weeps for his beloved. Vetala asks the king, who answers that a Brahmin is always to be honoured by the merchant class as the form of Brahman, and that Suvarna understood in his heart that his beloved was devoted to Brahmins.

06-021.json.summary: Vetala tells King Vikrama a humble tale. A Brahmin learned in the Vedas lives in a village and has four sons, each given to one of the four parts of life. By fate they lose their wealth, and ask their father why. He tells them gambling spends wealth and is the root of sin, tells one son to leave the company of courtesans and to give up meat and wine, and tells them all to turn to Lord Vishnu and give up unbelief and abuse of the gods. They go to another holy place, and after a year Shiva gives them the knowledge that revives the dead. They find a dead tiger's bones. One casts mantra-blessed water on them, the other pours milk, one pours water, and the unbeliever gives water to the sleeping tiger. Vetala asks who is the greatest fool, and the answer is the one who woke the tiger.

06-022.json.summary: Vetala tells of a Brahmin who is learned in the Vedas and has two sons skilled in all learning. An old man devoted to Shiva, Shambhudatta, makes a joyful fire offering. Liladhara sees a goat about to die and says killing creatures leads to a dreadful hell. He recalls that long ago in the Satya age, Brahmins performed sacrifices and spoke sweetly, but their view gave no fruit. The sages are amazed. In the Treta age the world became full of rajas, and he says gods are pleased by offerings, not by flesh and blood. A king named Kshatrasimha comes to Mohana, who tells of reciting the Saptashati and the goddess who creates and protects the world, and lists her powers such as Shachi, Siddhi, thirst, contentment, love, conduct, harm and patience. Kshatrasimha is tested by questions. The chapter says this is the time of Vikrama's story, and that a king will restore the holy places. Vetala vanishes and tells the sages, headed by Suta, that twilight has come.

06-023.json.summary: Vyasa tells that the sages lived in deep trance for a year. At that time King Vikramaditya is mentioned. The sages go to Suta and propose to have the king perform a horse sacrifice by his command. Suta comes with them. The horse goes to Kapila's place in the east and the bridge to Lanka in the south, and then to the Kshipra river. All the gods with their wives come to the king's sacrifice. After it the king gives many gifts, together with Vetala, and the moon gives nectar water and vanishes. The king gives the nectar to Indra, who goes to heaven. A Brahmin named Jayanta praises Bhartrihari for a hundred thousand gold pieces, and Vikramaditya rules without thorns. Shaunaka and the sages, knowing the king reached heaven, hear Suta recite the Puranas again.

06-024.json.summary: Vyasa asks Suta for something for people's good across the four ages. Suta begins with a salutation to Rama with Lakshmana and Sita.
